title: What if you left a glass of water on the Moon?
caption:
This water boils and freezes at the same time. 💧🌕

The Moon has almost no air: about 3×10⁻¹⁵ bar at night (NASA), against about 1 bar on Earth. Liquid water needs at least 611.657 Pa of pressure (its triple point), so an open glass boils even at room temperature.

Boiling pulls heat out of the water, so what's left freezes, and then the ice slowly turns straight into vapour too. Only the permanently dark polar craters, measured below −238 °C (−397 °F) by NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, are cold enough to keep ice.

Send this to the friend who always leaves a glass of water on the table.

Tomorrow: a balloon on Mars. 🔔 Follow @the.impossible.lab (or subscribe on YouTube) so you don't miss it.

⚠️ Don't try this. Vacuum chambers are lab equipment, not toys: glass under vacuum can implode.

sources: NASA NSSDC Moon Fact Sheet: surface pressure (night) 3 x 10^-15 bar (2 x 10^-12 torr); diurnal range 95-390 K - https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/moonfact.html

Harvard Natural Sciences Lecture Demonstrations: room-temperature water boils in an evacuated bell jar and then freezes due to rapid surface evaporation - https://sciencedemonstrations.fas.harvard.edu/presentations/boilingfreezing-water-vacuum
Univ. of Illinois Physics Van Q&A: evaporation cools the remaining water until it freezes; with continued pumping the ice itself sublimes - https://van.physics.illinois.edu/qa/listing.php?id=1597
Triple point of water: 611.657 Pa, 273.16 K (0.01 C) - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_point ; NIST kelvin realization - https://www.nist.gov/si-redefinition/kelvin-present-realization

Space.com (18 Sep 2009), LRO Diviner: minimum brightness temperatures in permanently shadowed polar craters below -397 F (about -238 C), craters suspected to harbor water ice - https://www.space.com/7311-moon-craters-coldest-place-solar-system.html
